_source: Branch Education Short 'How GPUs Are Printed With Light', watched in the built-in browser 2026-11-18: frames every ~3 s plus a 0.3 s burst at 31.7-32.7 s, sentence timings from the transcript panel (word counts only), sound measured with the yt-style probe over the whole Short. Our own descriptions.

hook.firstFrame: a graphics card floating and turning slowly on a grey-blue gradient, studio-lit
hook.firstLine: Inside this graphics card sits a chip built from billions of transistors

shots.picture: graphics card floating and rotating on a soft grey-blue gradient, rim-lit
the bare GPU package lifted out of the card, close up, blurred bright board behind
chip surface glowing rainbow; a giant transistor model hovers above it on a cone of light; neon count above
macro of gold wire layers stacked like a city grid, red particles drifting
a silicon wafer tilted on a dark grid floor; a glowing arc measures its width
a huge machine in a dark showroom; a neon handwritten price draws on above it
the camera dives through the machine's open side into its insides
violet light beam falling onto a wafer on a moving stage inside the machine
the wafer stage with a ring timer counting up beside it
pull back out of the machine; a neon number starts drawing
a tall stack of wafers on a starfield, chips spilling off the top
the wafer stack again with a small subscribe badge popping in above
a phone frame playing the channel's long video, subscribe badge above

lines.gist: points inside a graphics card at its chip and its transistor count
zooms to show the transistors with wiring stacked on top
the chip was made on a big wafer alongside dozens of others
names the very expensive light-printing machine that patterns it
the machine prints one layer of every chip on the wafer in seconds
so one machine turns out about half a million chips a day
points to the long video on the topic and asks for a subscribe

ending.cta: watch the long video on EUV and subscribe
ending.lastFrame: a phone frame playing the long video with a subscribe badge

whyItWorks: starts on a thing everyone recognises (a graphics card) and dives inward one scale at a time: card, chip, transistors, wafer, machine
every big figure is drawn as a glowing neon handwritten number in the 3D scene, not a flat caption card
the camera flies through the side of a machine into its working insides in under a second
studio-lit products on soft gradients and dark reflective floors keep every object readable on a phone
